TP2: Extensions to linear models — Correction

Author

Lionel Hertzog

Published

September 11, 2026

library(tidyverse)
library(DHARMa)
library(ggeffects)

1 Objectives

The aim of this practical is to explore several extensions of the linear model:

  1. Multiple covariates
  2. Interactions
  3. Variable transformations
  4. Polynomial terms

We continue working with forest biomass data from the Vosges, using an augmented dataset containing information on stand structure, elevation, soil properties, dominant tree species and ownership.

2 Read the data

We first load the dataset and perform a quick exploration.

here::i_am("practicals/tp2_correction.qmd")

The variables are:

  • idp: plot ID
  • mqd: square root of the mean quadratic diameter, a proxy for stand maturity, in m
  • biomass: above- and belowground tree biomass, in tonnes of dry matter per hectare
  • zp: elevation, in m
  • reserutile: soil water-holding capacity, in mm
  • troph_r: soil fertility proxy derived from the flora, ranging from 0 (acid soils) to 11 (calcareous soils)
  • species: dominant tree species
  • ownership: ownership status of the plot

There are some missing values in biomass and troph_r. For the regression analyses, we use complete observations for the variables included in each model.

A useful first look at the main numerical variables is:

dat %>%
  select(mqd, biomass, zp, reserutile, troph_r) %>%
  pairs()

3 Multiple covariates

3.1 1.1 Fit a model with several covariates

We first model biomass as a function of soil fertility, soil water-holding capacity and elevation:

\[ biomass = \beta_0 + \beta_1 troph_r + \beta_2 reserutile + \beta_3 zp + \epsilon. \]

# drop na for the needed covariables
dat_m1 <- dat %>%
  drop_na(biomass, troph_r, reserutile, zp)

# fit the model
m1 <- lm(
  biomass ~ troph_r + reserutile + zp,
  data = dat_m1
)

summary(m1)

Call:
lm(formula = biomass ~ troph_r + reserutile + zp, data = dat_m1)

Residuals:
    Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max 
-285.28  -94.88   -5.79   83.07  864.65 

Coefficients:
             Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept) 1.661e+02  8.296e+00  20.017  < 2e-16 ***
troph_r     1.366e+01  1.502e+00   9.093  < 2e-16 ***
reserutile  8.785e-02  6.791e-02   1.294    0.196    
zp          3.907e-02  9.989e-03   3.911 9.35e-05 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 130.8 on 3402 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.02945,   Adjusted R-squared:  0.02859 
F-statistic: 34.41 on 3 and 3402 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16

We then check the model assumptions with DHARMa:

res1 <- simulateResiduals(m1)

plot(res1)
plotResiduals(res1, form = fitted(m1))
plotResiduals(res1, form = dat_m1$troph_r) # this is testing the linearity of the relation

Interpretation.

The model explains only a relatively small proportion (3%) of the variation in biomass. The diagnostic plots should nevertheless be inspected before interpreting the coefficients.

The important point is that adding several covariates does not automatically make a model useful: we need to consider both the estimated effects and whether the model describes the data adequately.

3.2 1.2 Can we identify the most important covariate?

The raw regression coefficients cannot be directly compared because the three covariates are measured in very different units.

For example, troph_r is an index, reserutile is measured in mm, and zp is measured in metres.

A simple solution is to standardise the predictors before fitting the model:

m1_scaled <- lm(
  biomass ~ scale(troph_r) +
    scale(reserutile) +
    scale(zp),
  data = dat_m1
)

summary(m1_scaled)

Call:
lm(formula = biomass ~ scale(troph_r) + scale(reserutile) + scale(zp), 
    data = dat_m1)

Residuals:
    Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max 
-285.28  -94.88   -5.79   83.07  864.65 

Coefficients:
                  Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept)        232.238      2.241 103.653  < 2e-16 ***
scale(troph_r)      20.627      2.269   9.093  < 2e-16 ***
scale(reserutile)    2.933      2.267   1.294    0.196    
scale(zp)            8.769      2.242   3.911 9.35e-05 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 130.8 on 3402 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.02945,   Adjusted R-squared:  0.02859 
F-statistic: 34.41 on 3 and 3402 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16

The coefficients now correspond to a one-standard-deviation increase in each predictor.

For this dataset, the standardised coefficients show that soil fertility (troph_r) has the largest estimated effect, followed by elevation (zp), while the effect of water-holding capacity (reserutile) is considerably smaller.

We should, however, avoid interpreting coefficient magnitude alone as a complete measure of variable importance. Statistical uncertainty, ecological relevance and the amount of independent information provided by each variable also matter.

3.3 1.3 Effects of soil fertility under different environmental conditions

We can use predict_response() to visualise the expected biomass across the soil-fertility gradient while changing the values of the other covariates.

Here we use the mean ± one standard deviation as representative values:

reserutile_values <- with(
  dat_m1,
  mean(reserutile) + c(-1, 0, 1) * sd(reserutile)
)

zp_values <- with(
  dat_m1,
  mean(zp) + c(-1, 0, 1) * sd(zp)
)

terms_reserutile <- paste0(
  "reserutile [",
  paste(round(reserutile_values, 1), collapse = ","),
  "]"
)

terms_zp <- paste0(
  "zp [",
  paste(round(zp_values, 1), collapse = ","),
  "]"
)

pred_m1 <- predict_response(
  m1,
  terms = c("troph_r", terms_reserutile, terms_zp)
)

plot(pred_m1)

Because this model contains no interaction terms, the effect of troph_r is additive: changing reserutile or zp shifts the predicted biomass but does not change the slope of the relationship between biomass and troph_r (parallel lines).

4 Categorical covariates

4.1 2.1 Soil fertility and ownership

We now include ownership as a categorical covariate:

dat_m2 <- dat %>%
  drop_na(biomass, troph_r, ownership)

m2 <- lm(
  biomass ~ troph_r + ownership,
  data = dat_m2
)

summary(m2)

Call:
lm(formula = biomass ~ troph_r + ownership, data = dat_m2)

Residuals:
    Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max 
-282.86  -96.28   -6.15   83.19  879.80 

Coefficients:

(Intercept)                                  197.8119     5.8160  34.012
troph_r                                       14.6829     1.5753   9.321
ownershipForêts domaniales RF                 -6.9726     5.5650  -1.253
ownershipForêts privées et autres - En PSG    -0.8169     8.4170  -0.097
ownershipForêts privées et autres - Hors PSG -19.3356     6.0348  -3.204
                                             Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept)                                   < 2e-16 ***
troph_r                                       < 2e-16 ***
ownershipForêts domaniales RF                 0.21032    
ownershipForêts privées et autres - En PSG    0.92269    
ownershipForêts privées et autres - Hors PSG  0.00137 ** 
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 130.9 on 3401 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.0277,    Adjusted R-squared:  0.02656 
F-statistic: 24.23 on 4 and 3401 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16

By default, R uses one ownership class as the reference level. We can see the current ordering with:

levels(factor(dat_m2$ownership))
[1] "Autres forêts publiques RF"          "Forêts domaniales RF"               
[3] "Forêts privées et autres - En PSG"   "Forêts privées et autres - Hors PSG"

It is often preferable to choose the reference level explicitly:

dat_m2$ownership <- factor(
  dat_m2$ownership,
  levels = c(
    "Autres forêts publiques RF",
    "Forêts domaniales RF",
    "Forêts privées et autres - En PSG",
    "Forêts privées et autres - Hors PSG"
  )
)

m2 <- lm(
  biomass ~ troph_r + ownership,
  data = dat_m2
)

summary(m2)

Call:
lm(formula = biomass ~ troph_r + ownership, data = dat_m2)

Residuals:
    Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max 
-282.86  -96.28   -6.15   83.19  879.80 

Coefficients:
                                             Estimate Std. Error t value
(Intercept)                                  197.8119     5.8160  34.012
troph_r                                       14.6829     1.5753   9.321
ownershipForêts domaniales RF                 -6.9726     5.5650  -1.253
ownershipForêts privées et autres - En PSG    -0.8169     8.4170  -0.097
ownershipForêts privées et autres - Hors PSG -19.3356     6.0348  -3.204
                                             Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept)                                   < 2e-16 ***
troph_r                                       < 2e-16 ***
ownershipForêts domaniales RF                 0.21032    
ownershipForêts privées et autres - En PSG    0.92269    
ownershipForêts privées et autres - Hors PSG  0.00137 ** 
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 130.9 on 3401 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.0277,    Adjusted R-squared:  0.02656 
F-statistic: 24.23 on 4 and 3401 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16

The model coefficients are interpreted relative to the reference ownership class.

The coefficient for troph_r represents the expected change in biomass for a one-unit increase in soil fertility while holding ownership constant.

Each ownership coefficient represents the difference in expected biomass between that ownership class and the reference class, at the same value of troph_r.

For example, the coefficient for Forêts domaniales RF is the difference between state forests and the reference ownership class after accounting for soil fertility.

Importantly, this model does not allow the effect of soil fertility to differ among ownership classes. It assumes parallel regression lines.

4.2 2.2 Plot the predicted values

pred_m2 <- predict_response(
  m2,
  terms = c("troph_r", "ownership")
)

plot(pred_m2) +
  labs(
    x = "Soil fertility (troph_r)",
    y = "Predicted biomass (t DM/ha)"
  )

The four lines are parallel because the model contains no interaction between troph_r and ownership.

4.3 2.3 Bonus: changing contrasts

The choice of contrasts changes the parameterisation of the model, but not the fitted values.

For example, we can use treatment contrasts:

options(contrasts = c("contr.treatment", "contr.poly"))

m2_treatment <- lm(
  biomass ~ troph_r + ownership,
  data = dat_m2
)

coef(m2_treatment)
                                 (Intercept) 
                                 197.8119206 
                                     troph_r 
                                  14.6829219 
               ownershipForêts domaniales RF 
                                  -6.9726114 
  ownershipForêts privées et autres - En PSG 
                                  -0.8168649 
ownershipForêts privées et autres - Hors PSG 
                                 -19.3355904

We can instead use sum contrasts:

options(contrasts = c("contr.sum", "contr.poly"))

m2_sum <- lm(
  biomass ~ troph_r + ownership,
  data = dat_m2
)

coef(m2_sum)
(Intercept)     troph_r  ownership1  ownership2  ownership3 
191.0306539  14.6829219   6.7812667  -0.1913447   5.9644018

The numerical values of the coefficients change because their interpretation changes.

With treatment contrasts, the intercept corresponds to the reference ownership class.

With sum contrasts, the intercept corresponds to the grand mean across ownership levels (for a balanced interpretation of the factor), and the factor coefficients describe deviations from that overall mean.

The important result is:

predict(m2_treatment)[1:5]
       1        2        3        4        5 
234.6057 214.1722 237.9356 214.4353 225.7248 
predict(m2_sum)[1:5]
       1        2        3        4        5 
234.6057 214.1722 237.9356 214.4353 225.7248

The predictions are the same (up to numerical precision).

After this exercise, it is good practice to restore the default contrast settings:

options(contrasts = c("contr.treatment", "contr.poly"))

5 Interactions

An interaction allows the effect of one predictor to depend on another predictor.

5.1 1.1 Interaction between soil fertility and ownership

We now fit:

m3 <- lm(
  biomass ~ troph_r * ownership,
  data = dat_m2
)

summary(m3)

Call:
lm(formula = biomass ~ troph_r * ownership, data = dat_m2)

Residuals:
    Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max 
-284.44  -96.40   -6.24   82.92  880.54 

Coefficients:
                                                     Estimate Std. Error
(Intercept)                                           196.537      8.072
troph_r                                                15.125      2.501
ownershipForêts domaniales RF                         -13.324     11.936
ownershipForêts privées et autres - En PSG             -4.754     17.466
ownershipForêts privées et autres - Hors PSG           -6.581     13.603
troph_r:ownershipForêts domaniales RF                   3.040      4.349
troph_r:ownershipForêts privées et autres - En PSG      1.629      5.923
troph_r:ownershipForêts privées et autres - Hors PSG   -3.670      3.740
                                                     t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept)                                           24.348  < 2e-16 ***
troph_r                                                6.049 1.62e-09 ***
ownershipForêts domaniales RF                         -1.116    0.264    
ownershipForêts privées et autres - En PSG            -0.272    0.786    
ownershipForêts privées et autres - Hors PSG          -0.484    0.629    
troph_r:ownershipForêts domaniales RF                  0.699    0.485    
troph_r:ownershipForêts privées et autres - En PSG     0.275    0.783    
troph_r:ownershipForêts privées et autres - Hors PSG  -0.981    0.326    
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 130.9 on 3398 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.02842,   Adjusted R-squared:  0.02641 
F-statistic:  14.2 on 7 and 3398 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16

The * notation is equivalent to:

biomass ~ troph_r + ownership + troph_r:ownership

The interaction coefficients describe how the slope of troph_r changes for each ownership class relative to the reference class.

For the reference ownership class:

  • the intercept is the expected biomass when troph_r = 0;
  • the troph_r coefficient is the slope of biomass against soil fertility.

For another ownership class:

  • its ownership coefficient changes the intercept;
  • its interaction coefficient changes the slope.

Thus, for an ownership class with interaction coefficient \(\gamma\), its soil-fertility slope is:

\[ (\beta_1 + \gamma) * troph\_r \]

For this dataset, the estimated interaction terms are relatively small compared with the main effect of soil fertility. Their is therefore limited evidence for strong interactive effects between ownership class and soil fertility.

5.2 1.2 Plot the regression lines

pred_m3 <- predict_response(
  m3,
  terms = c("troph_r", "ownership")
)

plot(pred_m3) +
  labs(
    x = "Soil fertility (troph_r)",
    y = "Predicted biomass (t DM/ha)"
  )

Unlike the previous model, the lines are now allowed to have different slopes.

This is the key visual distinction between an additive model and an interaction model:

  • without interaction: parallel lines;
  • with interaction: slopes can differ.

6 Scaling and interactions

6.1 2.1 Scale soil fertility

We now standardise troph_r and fit the same interaction model:

m3_scaled <- lm(
  biomass ~ scale(troph_r) * ownership,
  data = dat_m2
)

summary(m3_scaled)

The coefficients are different because scale(troph_r) changes the units of the predictor.

However, the underlying fitted model is the same apart from the change of units. In particular, the fitted values are identical:

all.equal(
  fitted(m3),
  fitted(m3_scaled),
  tolerance = 1e-8
)
[1] TRUE

Scaling changes the interpretation of the coefficients, but not the information contained in the predictor or the fitted relationship.

6.2 2.2 Interaction between soil fertility and elevation

We now consider whether the relationship between soil fertility and biomass changes with elevation.

First, fit the model using the original soil-fertility variable:

dat_m4 <- dat %>%
  drop_na(biomass, troph_r, zp)

m4 <- lm(
  biomass ~ troph_r * zp,
  data = dat_m4
)

summary(m4)

---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 130.1 on 3402 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.03877,   Adjusted R-squared:  0.03792 
F-statistic: 45.74 on 3 and 3402 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16

The coefficients are not numerically identical because the unit of troph_r has changed.

For example, in the unscaled model, the interaction coefficient describes the change in the effect of one unit of troph_r associated with a one-metre increase in elevation.

After scaling, it describes the change in the effect of a one-standard-deviation increase in troph_r associated with a one-standard-deviation increase in elevation.

The fitted values, residuals and model fit are unchanged:

all.equal(
  fitted(m4),
  fitted(m4_scaled),
  tolerance = 1e-8
)
[1] TRUE

This illustrates an important property of scaling: it changes the parameterisation and interpretation of coefficients, but not the fitted relationship.

Scaling can nevertheless be very useful when interaction terms are present because it makes the main effects more interpretable and can reduce numerical problems when predictors are on very different scales.

7 Non-linear relations

Linear models can describe some non-linear relationships by transforming predictors or by adding polynomial terms.

7.1 Variable transformation

The relationship between biomass and elevation can be explored with a smooth curve:

ggplot(dat, aes(x = zp, y = biomass)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.25) +
  stat_smooth() +
  labs(
    x = "Elevation (m)",
    y = "Biomass (t DM/ha)"
  )

7.2 1. Which transformation is appropriate?

A saturating relationship is naturally represented by a logarithmic transformation:

\[ biomass = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \log(zp) + \epsilon. \]

The logarithm increases rapidly at low values of zp and progressively more slowly as zp increases, producing a saturating curve when expressed against the original elevation scale.

We can compare several possibilities visually:

ggplot(dat, aes(x = zp, y = biomass)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.25) +
  stat_smooth(
    method = "lm",
    formula = y ~ log(x)
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Elevation (m)",
    y = "Biomass (t DM/ha)"
  )

The logarithmic transformation is therefore a sensible choice here.

7.3 2. Fit the transformed model

We can fit the model directly in the formula:

dat_m5 <- dat %>%
  drop_na(biomass, zp)

m_log_zp <- lm(
  biomass ~ log(zp),
  data = dat_m5
)

summary(m_log_zp)

Call:
lm(formula = biomass ~ log(zp), data = dat_m5)

Residuals:
    Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max 
-243.60  -95.03   -9.71   81.88  879.57 

Coefficients:
            Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept)   98.714     35.934   2.747  0.00604 ** 
log(zp)       21.200      5.695   3.722  0.00020 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 132.4 on 3408 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.004049,  Adjusted R-squared:  0.003757 
F-statistic: 13.86 on 1 and 3408 DF,  p-value: 0.0002005

For comparison, fit the untransformed model:

m_linear_zp <- lm(
  biomass ~ zp,
  data = dat_m5
)

summary(m_linear_zp)

Call:
lm(formula = biomass ~ zp, data = dat_m5)

Residuals:
    Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max 
-246.45  -94.89   -9.24   82.21  881.18 

Coefficients:
            Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept) 210.9950     6.3384  33.288  < 2e-16 ***
zp            0.0362     0.0101   3.584 0.000343 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 132.4 on 3408 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.003756,  Adjusted R-squared:  0.003463

The logarithmic model is preferable to the straight-line model when the aim is specifically to represent a saturating relationship. However, the relationship in these data is relatively weak, R² is 0.003, so the transformation should not be interpreted as evidence of a strong ecological effect by itself.

7.4 3. Plot and compare the fitted relationships

pred_linear_zp <- predict_response(
  m_linear_zp,
  terms = "zp"
)

pred_log_zp <- predict_response(
  m_log_zp,
  terms = "zp"
)

plot(pred_linear_zp) +
  labs(
    x = "Elevation (m)",
    y = "Predicted biomass (t DM/ha)"
  )

and:

plot(pred_log_zp) +
  labs(
    x = "Elevation (m)",
    y = "Predicted biomass (t DM/ha)"
  )

The logarithmic model produces a curve whose slope decreases with elevation, whereas the untransformed model produces a straight line.

8 Polynomials

The relationship between stand maturity (mqd) and biomass appears hump-shaped:

ggplot(dat, aes(x = mqd, y = biomass)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.25) +
  stat_smooth() +
  labs(
    x = "Stand maturity (mqd)",
    y = "Biomass (t DM/ha)"
  )

A second-degree polynomial is appropriate for a simple hump-shaped relationship:

\[ biomass = \beta_0 + \beta_1 mqd + \beta_2 mqd^2 + \epsilon. \]

8.1 1. Compare linear and polynomial models

First fit the simple linear model:

dat_mqd <- dat %>%
  drop_na(biomass, mqd)

m_mqd_linear <- lm(
  biomass ~ mqd,
  data = dat_mqd
)

Then fit the quadratic model:

m_mqd_quad <- lm(
  biomass ~ mqd + I(mqd^2),
  data = dat_mqd
)

summary(m_mqd_quad)

Call:
lm(formula = biomass ~ mqd + I(mqd^2), data = dat_mqd)

Residuals:
    Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max 
-306.61  -69.46   -9.31   60.92  794.40 

Coefficients:
            Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept)  -125.13      10.86  -11.52   <2e-16 ***
mqd          2086.74      72.52   28.78   <2e-16 ***
I(mqd^2)    -2448.47     110.86  -22.09   <2e-16 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 111.2 on 3407 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.2979,    Adjusted R-squared:  0.2975 
F-statistic: 722.8 on 2 and 3407 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16

The quadratic model provides a much better description of the hump-shaped relationship than the simple linear model.

We can compare their DHARMa residuals:

res_mqd_linear <- simulateResiduals(m_mqd_linear)
res_mqd_quad <- simulateResiduals(m_mqd_quad)

plotResiduals(res_mqd_linear, form = dat_mqd$mqd)
plotResiduals(res_mqd_quad, form = dat_mqd$mqd)

The quadratic model removes much of the systematic curvature that remains in the residuals of the simple linear model.

We can also compare model fit using:

AIC(m_mqd_linear, m_mqd_quad)
             df      AIC
m_mqd_linear  3 42265.63
m_mqd_quad    4 41811.34
anova(m_mqd_linear, m_mqd_quad)
Analysis of Variance Table

Model 1: biomass ~ mqd
Model 2: biomass ~ mqd + I(mqd^2)
  Res.Df      RSS Df Sum of Sq     F    Pr(>F)    
1   3408 48131357                                 
2   3407 42103234  1   6028123 487.8 < 2.2e-16 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

A substantially lower AIC and a significant comparison support the quadratic model over the simple linear model.

A variable transformation could also be considered, but a quadratic polynomial is particularly convenient here because the relationship is explicitly hump-shaped: it can increase initially and then decrease.

8.2 2. Plot the selected model

pred_mqd_quad <- predict_response(
  m_mqd_quad,
  terms = "mqd"
)

plot(pred_mqd_quad) +
  labs(
    x = "Stand maturity (mqd)",
    y = "Predicted biomass (t DM/ha)"
  )

The fitted curve rises with mqd, reaches a maximum, and then decreases, producing the expected hump-shaped relationship.

8.3 3. Allow the non-linear relationship to vary with ownership

To investigate whether the quadratic relationship differs among ownership classes, we first standardise mqd.

dat_mqd$ownership <- factor(
  dat_mqd$ownership,
  levels = c(
    "Autres forêts publiques RF",
    "Forêts domaniales RF",
    "Forêts privées et autres - En PSG",
    "Forêts privées et autres - Hors PSG"
  )
)

dat_mqd$mqd_scaled <- as.numeric(
  scale(dat_mqd$mqd)
)

We can then include interactions between ownership and both polynomial terms:

m_mqd_ownership <- lm(
  biomass ~ (mqd_scaled + I(mqd_scaled^2)) * ownership,
  data = dat_mqd
)

summary(m_mqd_ownership)

8.4 4. Plot the regression lines

pred_mqd_ownership <- predict_response(
  m_mqd_ownership,
  terms = c("mqd_scaled", "ownership")
)

plot(pred_mqd_ownership) +
  labs(
    x = "Scaled stand maturity (mqd)",
    y = "Predicted biomass (t DM/ha)"
  )

The resulting curves can look unusual, particularly near the edges of the predictor range.

This is a common danger when fitting interactions involving polynomial terms: each ownership class is given its own quadratic curve, and the model can therefore predict very different behaviour where there are few or no observations.

The most important point is that we should not interpret predictions outside the range of the data for a given ownership class -> linear model have poor extrapolation capacities.

We can check the range of mqd within each ownership class:

dat_mqd %>%
  group_by(ownership) %>%
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    min_mqd = min(mqd),
    max_mqd = max(mqd)
  )
# A tibble: 4 × 4
  ownership                               n min_mqd max_mqd
  <fct>                               <int>   <dbl>   <dbl>
1 Autres forêts publiques RF           1300  0.0811   0.752
2 Forêts domaniales RF                 1034  0.0813   0.692
3 Forêts privées et autres - En PSG     299  0.0844   0.714
4 Forêts privées et autres - Hors PSG   777  0.0764   0.563

8.5 How can we remedy this?

A first remedy is to restrict predictions to the range of mqd that is actually observed within each ownership class rather than extrapolating the quadratic curves beyond the data.

It is also useful to display the observations together with the fitted curves:

ggplot(dat_mqd, aes(x = mqd_scaled, y = biomass, colour = ownership)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.15) +
  geom_smooth(
    method = "lm",
    formula = y ~ x + I(x^2),
    se = FALSE
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Scaled stand maturity (mqd)",
    y = "Biomass (t DM/ha)"
  )

This makes it much easier to distinguish a genuine pattern supported by observations from a model-driven extrapolation.

More generally, when fitting complex interactions, we should always ask:

  • Do we have data across the predictor gradient for every group?
  • Are some predictions extrapolations?
  • Is the additional complexity ecologically justified?
  • Does the more complex model substantially improve the description of the data?

9 Summary

This practical illustrates three important extensions of the simple linear model.

9.1 Multiple covariates

Adding several predictors allows us to estimate the association between one predictor and the response while controlling for the others.

9.2 Interactions

Interactions allow the effect of one predictor to depend on another predictor. Graphically, interactions produce regression lines with different slopes rather than necessarily parallel lines.

9.3 Transformations and polynomials

A linear model does not necessarily imply a straight-line relationship with the original predictor. Transformations such as log(x) and polynomial terms such as x + x^2 allow us to describe curved relationships while retaining the linear-model framework.

Finally, increasingly complex models require increasingly careful checking of their predictions. In particular, interactions and polynomial terms can produce apparently plausible curves in regions where there are little or no observations, so extrapolation should always be checked explicitly - this applies also to other model types than regression models such as machine learning models.
